name: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies
description: Systems and measurements for user privacy: tracking, anonymization, private data sharing, and privacy on the web/mobile.
narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, from 2018, already split into the two camps that define privacy-enhancing technologies research. On one side sits empirical measurement of how the real world tracks and monetizes users: "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators" (NDSS 2018) mapped the mobile tracking ecosystem at global scale, "FP-STALKER" (S&P 2018) showed how browser fingerprints evolve and can be re-linked over time, and "Privacy Risks with Facebook's PII-Based Targeting" (S&P 2018) audited an ad platform to show how data brokers leak personal information. Alongside this, "Polisis" (USENIX 2018) used deep learning to make opaque privacy policies machine-readable. On the other side sits the cryptographic/systems camp building private primitives: "PIR with Compressed Queries" (S&P 2018) and "Oblix" (S&P 2018) pushed practical private retrieval and oblivious search, while a cluster of searchable-encryption work and the "Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data" (S&P 2018) sharpened the cat-and-mouse game between encrypted-database designs and leakage-abuse attacks.

The arrival of GDPR in 2018 reoriented the measurement side toward law and compliance. "(Un)informed Consent" (CCS 2019) and later "Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice?" (S&P 2020) turned cookie-consent notices into objects of rigorous measurement, while policy-analysis tools "PolicyLint" (USENIX 2019) and "PoliCheck" (USENIX 2020) moved from reading policies to catching apps whose behavior contradicts their stated promises. In parallel, differential privacy shifted from theory to deployable systems: "PrivKV" (S&P 2019) and the decentralized graph work at CCS 2019 advanced local DP for real data collection, and the "Private Summation in the Multi-Message Shuffle Model" (CCS 2020) and "Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters" (S&P 2021) refined the shuffle-model and heavy-hitter primitives behind industrial telemetry.

A defining breakthrough of this period was the realization that privacy threats and defenses both increasingly run through machine learning. Website-fingerprinting attacks went deep-learning and portable with "Triplet Fingerprinting" (CCS 2019), prompting defenses like "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses" (USENIX 2020) and a sober real-world re-evaluation in "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022). Most strikingly, "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020) inverted the usual framing by using adversarial perturbations to protect ordinary people from facial-recognition scraping. Research also widened beyond the browser to cyber-physical and human contexts: side-channel privacy attacks on smartphone motion sensors ("Speechless," S&P 2018), 4G/5G paging ("Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols," NDSS 2019), smart-home traffic ("Packet-Level Signatures," NDSS 2020), AR ("Towards Security and Privacy for Multi-user Augmented Reality," S&P 2018), and the deeply human work on intimate-partner-violence victims ("Clinical Computer Security," USENIX 2019).

Where the area stands now reflects two trends. First, generative AI is reshaping both threat and defense, with "Glaze" (USENIX 2023) extending the Fawkes idea to shield artists from style mimicry by text-to-image models. Second, the cryptographic camp is delivering deployable anonymity primitives that plug into real identity systems, as with "zk-creds" (S&P 2023), which builds flexible anonymous credentials from zkSNARKs atop existing infrastructure. Taken together, the field has matured from documenting and measuring privacy loss toward building practical, ML-aware countermeasures and provably private systems that interoperate with the messy reality of the web, mobile, and AI ecosystems.

milestones.title: Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning
milestones.note: pioneered using deep learning to make opaque privacy policies machine-readable, seeding a wave of automated policy analysis

milestones.title: Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data Using Range Query Leakage
milestones.note: crystallized the leakage-abuse attack threat that drove the encrypted-database arms race for years

milestones.title: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field
milestones.note: turned post-GDPR cookie-consent notices into a measurable object, launching the legal-compliance measurement line

milestones.title: Triplet Fingerprinting: More Practical and Portable Website Fingerprinting with N-shot Learning
milestones.note: brought few-shot deep learning to website fingerprinting, making the attack far more practical against Tor

milestones.title: Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models
milestones.note: flipped adversarial ML into a personal defense against facial-recognition scraping, a paradigm shift for user-side protection

milestones.title: Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters
milestones.note: advanced practical private aggregation primitives underpinning real-world differentially private telemetry

milestones.title: Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models
milestones.note: extended protective perturbations to the generative-AI era, defending creators against text-to-image style mimicry

milestones.title: zk-creds: Flexible Anonymous Credentials from zkSNARKs and Existing Identity Infrastructure
milestones.note: delivered deployable anonymous credentials via zkSNARKs that interoperate with existing identity systems
